list.listitem: Fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) defects are permanent and may prevent affected individuals from living independently. B

High rates of co-morbid conditions are found in children with FAS including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), oppositional defiant disorder, conduct disorder, autism spectrum disorders and mood disorders. B
The USPSTF recommends screening and providing behavioral counseling interventions to reduce alcohol misuse by adults, including pregnant women, in primary care settings. B
Behavioral interventions in women of childbearing age or pregnant women decrease alcohol use. The effects of a brief intervention are enhanced when a partner participates. A

Refer affected children as early as possible for multidisciplinary assessment. Earlier intervention is associated with improved outcomes in terms of school completion, mood disorders, and involvement with law enforcement. B

Multiple interventions are recommended including physical and occupational therapy and possibly medications to assist with managing attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), sleep disruption, mood disorders, and impulse disorders. B

background.definition: FAS is a birth defect characterized by selected facial malformations, growth retardation, central nervous system (CNS) abnormalities, and associated with maternal alcohol consumption during pregnancy. The disabilities are lifelong and impact multiple areas of the individual's life. Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASDs) are a group of physical, cognitive, and/or behavioral conditions that can occur in a person whose mother drank alcohol during pregnancy; FAS is the most severe condition in this group.

list.listitem: Using the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) FAS estimates, 1000 to 6000 children will be born with FAS in the United States annually.
Disadvantaged groups, Native Americans, and other minorities have been documented to have incidence rates as high as 3 to 5 FAS-affected children per 1000 children.
Prevalence of FAS varies from 0.2 to 1.5 cases per 1000 births in various populations. Estimates of FASD range from 1% to 5% of the US population, according to the CDC.

More recent data from a population study of first-grade students and their mothers in a Midwestern US community provided estimates of prevalence of FAS ranging from 6 to 9 per 1000 children. The total rate of FASD was estimated at 24 to 48 per 1000 children. These rates are significantly higher than previous population estimates. This study was conducted across an age cohort of students who were in public and private schools and not previously identified as having special needs.

This higher rate was confirmed in a population study of 6639 first-graders in 4 US communities; conservative prevalence estimates of FAC ranged from 11.3 (95% CI 7.8-15.8) to 50.0 (95% CI 39.9-61.7) per 1000 children.

Authors of a systematic review of 24 studies including 1416 children and youths found prevalence rates of FASD varied from a high of 19.8 (95% CI 14.1-28.0) per 1000 population in the WHO European region to 0.1 (95% CI 0.1-0.5) per 1000 population in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region. The highest rates were in South Africa (111.1 per 1000 population), Croatia (53.3 per 1000 population) and Ireland (47.5 per 1000 population).

Subpopulations of children such as those in care, correctional, special education, specialized clinical and Aboriginal populations have rates of FASD that are 10-40 times higher than the general population (7.7 per 1000, 95% CI 4.9-11.7), based on a meta-analysis of 69 studies with 6177 individuals diagnosed with FASD from 17 countries.

According to the CDC, the lifetime cost for one individual with FAS in 2002 was estimated to be $2 million. In contrast, authors of a systematic review estimated that one case of FASD can be prevented for an estimated $20,200 to $47,615.

In a Canadian study, the annual short-term economic cost for fetal alcohol spectrum disorders in Alberta was between $48 to $143 million (daily cost $105-$316 thousand) and the annual long-term economic cost from the disorders rose from $130 to $400 million.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found higher rates of comorbid disorders among children with FAS than the general population including ADHD (52.9%), Oppositional Defiant Disorder (12.9%), Conduct Disorder (7.0%), and ASD (2.6%).
Mental health problems such as anxiety and depression also appear to be associated with FAS.
Maternal alcohol consumption during pregnancy.

Light alcohol consumption (up to 10 g, about 1 drink daily) is not associated with an increased risk of low birthweight or small-for-gestational age (SGA) infants. Intake of up to 18 g daily does not affect the risk of prematurity. Dose-response gradients for low birthweight, premature birth, and SGA infants are seen above those amounts.

In a genetic study of 95 children with FAS, rare copy number variations, both genic and intergenic (between genes), were found in 90% and half had rare CNVs impacting coding sequences. Twelve children carried genic CNVs that might contribute to the etiology of FAS, including CACNA1H involved in epilepsy and autism. The authors recommend genetic testing of children with FAS for chromosomal deletions and duplications that may co-occur or explain the neurodevelopmental impairments.
Alcohol causes neuronal damage and cell loss in the fetal brain through direct action as a toxin.
Alcohol causes measurable damage specifically to the corpus callosum.

In one study, children exposed to prenatal alcohol compared to controls had higher DNA methylation and reduced expression of proopiomelanocortin, a precursor polypeptide synthesized in corticotrophs of the anterior pituitary, and period 2, a protein-coding gene considered a circadian pacemaker, along with increased levels of stress hormone cortisol and adrenocorticotropic hormone. Exposure also alters expression of angiogenesis-related proteins and cytokines in the placenta.
Neurologic development is ongoing throughout the pregnancy; therefore, there is no "safe" time for alcohol consumption.
The USPSTF (2018) recommends screening and providing behavioral counseling interventions to reduce alcohol misuse by adults, including pregnant women, in primary care settings. B
Two screening tools that have been specifically developed and used with pregnant women are the T-ACE and the TWEAK. B

Authors of a Cochrane review found evidence from a limited number of studies that psychological and educational interventions may result in increased abstinence from alcohol and a reduction in alcohol consumption among pregnant women; results, however, were not consistent. B

The USPSTF (2018) recommends screening and providing behavioral counseling interventions to reduce alcohol misuse by adults, including pregnant women, in primary care settings. The Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (2020) also recommend use of validated screening tools and brief intervention approaches to increase obstetrical care provider recognition of alcohol consumption and problematic alcohol use among women of child-bearing age and those who are pregnant.
The five-item TWEAK test is recommended as a screening questionnaire to identify heavy drinking or alcohol abuse and dependence in racially-mixed populations of nonpregnant and pregnant women ().

Meconium fatty acid ethyl esters, products of nonoxidative ethanol metabolism, have been suggested as a biomarker of maternal alcohol use; in a Canadian surveillance study, a higher percentage of the population was identified as having significant prenatal ethanol exposure than postpartum questionnaires in the same population (2.5% vs 0.5%).
Inform potential mothers of the potential for FAS, as well as the more minor manifestations of alcohol exposure on the infant and attention and learning problems in the growing child.

Brief interventions for prenatal alcohol use reduced subsequent consumption most significantly for women with the highest consumption initially. The effects of the brief intervention were significantly enhanced when a partner (any supportive adult) participated.

Among 200 pregnant substance users, including 41 women also using alcohol, motivational interviewing was helpful in reducing illicit-drug use days during the active and follow-up phases and alcohol use during the follow-up phase.
Key facial features to identify FAS (shortened palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, and thin vermillion border of upper lip) are more evident in infancy and early childhood. B
Consider referral of the child for multidisciplinary evaluation if able to identify a high-risk maternal alcohol history (more than 7 drinks per week or 3 or more drinks on multiple occasions). B

Be prepared for changes in clinical presentation across development. Cognitive delays and evidence of neurologic abnormalities may become more obvious and trigger a later recognition of the diagnosis. B

list.listitem: See for diagnostic criteria.
Infants may present with sleep cycle problems, poor muscle tone, or feeding problems (poor suck, texture aversion). They can also exhibit both prenatal and postnatal growth deficits.

Besides the key dysmorphic features (), other findings may include a flat midface, ptosis of the eyelids, epicanthal folds, an upturned nose with a flat nasal bridge, underdeveloped ears, clinodactyly of the fifth fingers, camptodactyly (flexion contracture of a finger or toe), "hockey stick" palmar creases, hirsutism, and cardiac defects.
Facial dysmorphic features are most evident during infancy and early preschool years, while cognitive and neurologic problems persist and are expressed as the patient grows.
Growth deficits: height or weight or head circumference less than the 10th percentile.

CNS abnormalities: decreased head circumference, brain structural anomaly observable through imaging, neurologic problems including seizures or cerebral palsy, visual motor difficulties, nystagmus, or overall problems with motor control, global cognitive deficit (eg, decreased Intelligence quotient [IQ]), significant developmental delay, or deficits in three or more specific functional domains. Without a known maternal alcohol history, several combinations of criteria can still justify referral.
Slightly older infants could display delayed motor skills.
Preschool period: delayed milestones, especially early language acquisition; attention problems and hyperactivity can emerge.
School age: problems with social perception skills, hyperactivity, poor sleep, and cognitive delays. Mathematics is often an area of severe delay.
Concerns may be raised by a variety of sources, particularly preschool or school personnel, if the child is not already identified as having FAS.
Adolescents may present with extreme intermittent explosive episodes, depression and suicidal ideation, inappropriate sexual behavior, and problems with substance abuse.
Adults may have panic attacks when cognitive capabilities are overwhelmed by life tasks. In addition, trouble with impulse-aggression control may lead to problems with law enforcement.

Measure height and weight and plot on standard growth curves. Use the WHO growth charts for children from birth to 2 years and the CDC growth charts for children and teenagers aged 2 to 19 years. Use preterm growth curves if the child was born preterm.
Examine child's face for smooth philtrum and thin vermillion border. Compare with Lip-Philtrum Guides found at www.depts.washington.edu/fasdpn/htmls/lip-philtrum-guides.htm.

Measure palpebral fissure length. Measurement technique can be viewed at www.depts.washington.edu/fasdpn/htmls/fas-tutor.htm. Live measurement technique is more accurate than 2 dimensional photographic assessment.

Compare palpebral fissure length with norms for Caucasian, Black, and Hispanic children found at www.fas.academicedge.com/documents/phyevalp.pdf. The measurement is consistent with FAS if less than the 10th percentile.

The facial features are the key physical examination features "accessible" to the physician in a standard clinical encounter. With training, the physician can learn to identify these features with fair-to-moderate agreement with dysmorphologists. A computer-aided assessment of facial features from photographs was comparable to in-person assessment in one study and might be useful for early recognition of FAS and alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder.

If 2 of the 3 cardinal facial characteristics are present (short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, and/or thin vermillion border of the upper lip), the child is classified as having a positive dysmorphology evaluation for FASD.
Multidisciplinary teams will complete evaluations of language, cognitive, and motor skills.
Biomarkers of FAS, including infant plasma extracellular, circulating miRNAs, are under investigation.
See for typical dysmorphic features and referral guidelines for multidisciplinary evaluation.
gives a recommended framework for management of the child with suspected FAS.
To identify referral resources, see the National and State Resource Directory at https://nofas.org/resource-directory/.

The facial phenotype of FAS is also observed in a variety of genetic and teratogenic conditions. Genetic testing may be needed to distinguish between diagnoses. A chromosome microarray has been shown to be the highest yield diagnostic test when a genetic phenocopy of FASD is being considered.

Multidisciplinary treatment is best, including a geneticist, a developmental pediatrician, a mental health professional, a social worker, physical and occupational therapists, and an educational specialist. B
The prognosis is best if the child is referred for treatment before the age of 6 years. B
The family will likely need ongoing counseling and respite services. B
Medications may be necessary in managing sleep disruption issues, ADHD symptoms, mood disorders, and impulse disorder and aggression. B
Pharmacotherapy can be useful and is indicated for ADHD, depression and mood swings, sleep problems, and impulse disorder and aggression.
Specific data on pharmacologic treatment of ADHD in children with FAS are limited.
Small pilot studies have been performed indicating that methylphenidate is well tolerated and provides for some modest improvements in ADHD symptoms in children identified as having FAS.
Risperidone has been shown to be a reasonable adjunct therapy, in addition to stimulant medications, in children with treatment-resistant aggression and ADHD.

Choline has been studied as a supplement in children ages 5-10 years with FASDs. It was not shown to result in improvement in cognitive function in any domain, despite excellent treatment adherence. In a 4-year follow-up of 31 children with FASD originally randomized to choline vs placebo at age 2 to 5 years, children who received choline had higher non-verbal intelligence, higher visual-spatial skill and working memory ability, better verbal memory, and fewer behavioral symptoms of ADHD than the placebo group.

Structured exercise programs, including yoga, have been shown to produce some improvement in attention task scores and in parent ratings of ADHD symptoms. Children who were receiving medications in addition to exercise therapy exhibited greater improvement.

An exercise program consisting of two 1.5-hr sessions/week for 8 weeks resulted in improved T scores on the Children's Color Trails Test, a neuropsychological test that measures attention, divided attention, and speed of mental processing, compared to children on a wait list. Improvement was sustained at 3 months.

Children with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) who participated in social skills training showed clear evidence of improvement in their knowledge of appropriate social behavior post treatment, and this improvement was maintained over a 3-month period. This program was a structured parent-assisted child friendship training.

Authors of an overview of five specific intervention research studies for individuals with FASD stressed the importance of parent education or training, teaching children specific skills they would usually learn by observation or abstraction, and integration into existing systems of treatment.

Authors of a systematic review of 25 RCTs also concluded that combination parent and child sessions presented a promising approach for the treatment of FASD. Benefits appear to be domain specific, however, with the exception of interventions regarding self-regulation or social interaction.

In a pilot RCT of 30 children ages 4 to 8 years with FASD or prenatal alcohol exposure, use of a 30-week intervention of bimonthly in-home parent behavioral consultation and weekly child skills groups improved child emotion regulation, self-esteem, and anxiety and caregiver knowledge and parenting efficacy over an active control of neuropsychological assessment and personalized community referrals; children in both groups improved with respect to disruptive behavior.

In a RCT of 44 children with FASD, direct current stimulation augmented cognitive training was well tolerated and improved attention on a continuous performance test compared to cognitive training alone, but there were no differences in other measures.

In a small RCT, a brief mathematics education intervention improved 6-month math skills and both the math intervention and control group intervention (psychoeducation) improved 6-month behavioral outcomes over baseline.
Due to the unknown extent of brain damage, refer for neurocognitive testing, occupational therapy evaluation, and physical therapy evaluation.
Due to the complexity of mood disorders, ADHD, and impulse-aggression problems, psychiatric referral may be needed.

As adolescents and adults, individuals with FAS experience high rates of "secondary disabilities" including school disruption, trouble with the law, mental health difficulties, alcohol/drug problems, and inability to live independently B (Final Report to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Grant No. R04/ccr008515, 1996).

The odds of escaping these adverse life outcomes are increased by two- to fourfold by two "protective" factors—receiving the diagnosis of FAS at an earlier age and being reared in good, stable environments; therefore, services to support the family are crucial. B
Lifetime disabilities impair functioning to the extent that they may prevent independent living.
A high prevalence of mood disorders, school problems, and problems with law enforcement is seen.
Reproductive effects have also been reported including delayed menarche and altered testosterone levels, reduced testes and accessory gland weights and reduced sperm concentration and semen volume.
Prognosis is improved with early identification, multiple services, and family support.
The family will need ongoing support and counseling to develop the specific parenting skills for raising a child affected by FAS.
Due to delayed transition and impairments, adolescents and young adults require transitional planning and possibly structured housing and vocational training.
No known safe amount of alcohol can be drunk during pregnancy.
The highest likelihood of complete FAS occurs with binge drinking (5 or more drinks per occasion).

Even small amounts of alcohol (1 ounce per day) have been linked to decreased IQ. A systematic review found that alcohol consumption (up to 10 g, about 1 drink daily) does not affect the risk of low birthweight or small-for-gestational age (SGA) infants. Intake of up to 18 g daily does not affect the risk of prematurity. Dose-response gradients for low birthweight, premature birth, and SGA infants are seen above those amounts.
If a woman is trying to get pregnant or is actively having unprotected sex, instruct her to abstain from alcohol.
A woman who is not abstaining from alcohol should see a health care provider about contraception.
Ask the woman to be honest about exposures to the baby.

Financial assistance may be available. A diagnosis of FAS is considered a "presumptive eligibility" diagnosis under Part C of the "Individuals with Disabilities Education Act." Presumptive diagnoses allow children under the age of 3 years who are at risk of later developmental delay to be served without meeting particular eligibility criteria.

cell.label: Child presents for office visit. Triggers emerge from contact, ie, developmental problems, facial abnormalities associated with FAS, growth delay, or maternal alcohol use.
Complete initial evaluation to gather specific data related to the four FAS criteria: facial malformations, growth abnormalities, neurodevelopmental concerns, maternal alcohol use.
Refer to specialist for further assessment.

FAS diagnosis confirmed using dysmorphic and anthropometric assessment procedures along with appropriate neurodevelopmental evaluation data. An intervention plan is developed using a multidisciplinary team approach.

The intervention plan is communicated to frontline providers, caregivers, and child with ongoing exchange with the intervention team. A case management plan is initiated at the community level based on recommendations from the intervention team (ie, specialty services, community and educational resources.)
Continue to monitor changes in child's health over time.

feature.caption: The TWEAK Score for Alcoholism Screening in Pregnancy.

list.listitem: (1A) How many drinks does it take before you begin to feel the first effects of alcohol? (3 or more drinks = 2 points)
(1B) How many drinks does it take before the alcohol makes you fall asleep or pass out? If you never pass out, what is the largest number of drinks that you have? (5 or more drinks = 2 points)
(2) Have your friends or relatives worried about your drinking in the past year? (Yes = 1 point)
(3) Do you sometimes take a drink in the morning when you first get up? (Yes = 1 point)
(4) Are there times when you drink and afterwards can not remember what you said or did? (Yes = 1 point)

Scoring: Three or more points is considered positive for alcoholism/heavy drinking. From Chan AW, Pristach EA, Welte JW, Russell M. Use of the TWEAK test in screening for alcoholism/heavy drinking in three populations. Alcohol Clin Exp Res 1993;17:1188-1192. (5) Do you sometimes feel the need to cut down on your drinking? (Yes = 1 point)

feature.caption: Referral Guidelines for Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders.
feature.feature_body:
If known prenatal alcohol exposure, meeting the following criteria, refer for complete evaluation by multidisciplinary FAS team.
Maternal alcohol exposure of 7 or more drinks per week or 3 or more drinks on multiple occasions
If unknown prenatal alcohol exposure, refer for multidisciplinary evaluation if any of the following conditions apply:
Caregiver or parental concern about possible FAS or Presence of all three of the following facial features:or
Smooth philtrum Thin vermillion border of the upper lip Small palpebral fissures
Presence of one or more facial features in addition to deficit in height or weight or Presence of one or more facial features in addition to CNS abnormalities Data from National Task Force on Fetal Alcohol Syndrome and Fetal Alcohol Effect. http://depts.washington.edu/fasdpn/htmls/lip-philtrum-guides.htm. FAS Diagnostic and Prevention Network.
